question: Electric vehicles (EVs) and the electrification of road transport have an important role to play in reducing greenhouse gas emissions. At the same time, certain challenges, such as the lack of charging infrastructure, high electricity charges (or even power supply issues) and the high initial cost of EVs need to be addressed in order to accelerate EV adoption. In this regard: 1.
How is the Commission working with the Member States to promote the growth of a more affordable EV market while ensuring that transport decarbonisation targets are met?

Has there been an assessment of the raw materials used for EV batteries and a comparison of the sustainability of hybrid cars or an analysis of who will bear the cost of replacing old vehicles with new ones?
answer: 1. As demand is expanding globally, the price of zero-emission vehicles is decreasing due to economies of scale. Several Member States have put in place measures to improve the affordability of such vehicles, which contributes to meeting their Effort Sharing Regulation (1) targets. The Social Climate Fund (2) will also contribute to supporting the affordability of those vehicles.

The Alternative Fuels Infrastructure Regulation (3) will ensure a minimum level of sufficient recharging and refuelling infrastructure throughout the EU that will enable seamless travel with zero-emission vehicles everywhere in the EU. The Commission will report every two years on the progress made in the transition to zero-emission mobility (4). 2.

The Critical Raw Materials Regulation (5) aims to ensure access to raw materials needed for the key technologies for the green transition. It was developed based on an impact assessment taking into account the expected needs in relation to electric vehicle batteries. The Commission will monitor the projected consumption of such materials and the impacts thereof, and report on it.
The social impacts of the shift to zero-emission vehicles have been considered in the impact assessment for the CO2 standards (6). Those impacts will continue to be monitored in the coming years.

The Commission is also developing a methodology to assess the lifecycle CO 2 emissions of vehicles, including hybrids, and a methodology for the calculation and verification of the carbon footprint of electric vehicle batteries (7). In addition, the proposed circularity requirements for vehicles include measures to increase collection, use of spare parts and quality recycling like recycled content targets (8).
